## 求解

我们需要求出满足以下方程的 $k$：
$$\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\ln x}{1-x}\right)^{2}dx+k\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\ln(1-x)}{x}\,dx=0.$$

设 $I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{(\ln x)^{2}}{(1-x)^{2}}\,dx$ 且 $L=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\ln(1-x)}{x}\,dx$。

### 第二个积分 $L$

使用 $\ln(1-x)=-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{x^{n}}{n}$，对于 $x\in(0,1)$，在 $(0,1)$ 上逐项积分得到
$$L=-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}\int_{0}^{1}x^{n-1}\,dx=-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}=-\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}.$$

### 第一个积分 $I$

将其在 $x=1$ 处拆分为 $[0,1]\cup[1,\infty)$。对于 $[1,\infty)$ 上的部分，代入 $x=1/t$，$dx=-dt/t^{2}$：
$$\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{(\ln x)^{2}}{(1-x)^{2}}\,dx=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(\ln t)^{2}}{(1-t)^{2}}\,dt.$$
（因为 $\ln x=-\ln t$，$(1-x)^{2}=(1-1/t)^{2}=(t-1)^{2}/t^{2}$，且测度 $dx=-dt/t^{2}$ 消去了因子 $t^{2}$。）

因此，设 $J=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(\ln t)^{2}}{(1-t)^{2}}\,dt$，我们有 $I=2J$。

### 计算 $J$

对于 $t\in(0,1)$，有 $\dfrac{1}{(1-t)^{2}}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n\,t^{n-1}$。通过单调收敛（被积函数非负）进行逐项积分：
$$J=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n\int_{0}^{1}t^{n-1}(\ln t)^{2}\,dt.$$
标准公式 $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}t^{a-1}(\ln t)^{m}\,dt=\frac{(-1)^{m}\,m!}{a^{m+1}}$（$a>0$）给出 $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}t^{n-1}(\ln t)^{2}\,dt=\frac{2}{n^{3}}$。因此
$$J=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n\cdot\frac{2}{n^{3}}=2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}=2\cdot\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{3}.$$
所以 $I=2J=\dfrac{2\pi^{2}}{3}$。

### 求解 $k$

该方程变为
$$\frac{2\pi^{2}}{3}+k\!\left(-\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\right)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{2\pi^{2}}{3}=\frac{k\,\pi^{2}}{6}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=\frac{2\pi^{2}}{3}\cdot\frac{6}{\pi^{2}}=4.$$

### 结论

$$\boxed{k=4}$$

Let me compute this. Let I = ∫₀^∞ (ln x)² / (1-x)² dx.

Note there's a singularity at x=1. Let me check convergence. Near x=1, ln x ≈ x-1, so (ln x)²/(1-x)² ≈ 1, integrable. At x→∞, (ln x)²/x² integrable. At x→0, (ln x)² integrable. So converges.

J = ∫₀^1 (ln t)² Σ_{n=1}^∞ n t^{n-1} dt = Σ_{n=1}^∞ n ∫₀^1 t^{n-1} (ln t)² dt.

∫₀^1 t^{n-1} (ln t)² dt = 2/n³ (standard result: ∫₀^1 t^{a-1} (ln t)^k dt = (-1)^k k!/a^{k+1}).

So J = Σ_{n=1}^∞ n · 2/n³ = 2 Σ_{n=1}^∞ 1/n² = 2 · π²/6 = π²/3.

Therefore I = 2J = 2π²/3.

Now the equation: I + k · (-π²/6) = 0
2π²/3 + k·(-π²/6) = 0
2π²/3 = k·π²/6
k = (2π²/3)·(6/π²) = 4.

So k = 4.

Let me verify the integration by parts / the I = 2J step more carefully.

Actually, let me double-check the substitution. I = ∫₀^∞ (ln x)²/(1-x)² dx = ∫₀^1 + ∫₁^∞.

The ∫₁^∞ part: x = 1/t. dx = -dt/t². 1-x = 1-1/t = (t-1)/t. (1-x)² = (t-1)²/t². (ln x)² = (ln(1/t))² = (ln t)².

So (ln x)²/(1-x)² dx = (ln t)² · t²/(t-1)² · (-dt/t²) = -(ln t)²/(t-1)² dt.

Limits: x: 1→∞ maps to t: 1→0. So ∫₁^∞ = ∫₁^0 -(ln t)²/(t-1)² dt = ∫₀^1 (ln t)²/(t-1)² dt = ∫₀^1 (ln t)²/(1-t)² dt = J. ✓

So I = J + J = 2J = 2π²/3. ✓

Equation: 2π²/3 - k·π²/6 = 0 → k = 4.

The answer is k = 4.
